newsitem.title: FRANCE: Poland eyes lower grain, wheat imports in 1996/97.
newsitem.headline: Poland eyes lower grain, wheat imports in 1996/97.

text.p: Poland will produce less grain but also import less from the world market in 1996/97 (July/June), due mainly to lower domestic demand for feed grain, a senior Polish food official said on Monday.

"1996 was not a good year for the crop but we expect to import less grain than in the past season mostly because of lower demand for feed grain," Ryszard Kreft, director general of the Agricultural Market Agency (ARR), told Reuters.

Poland's grain crop is thought to have fallen by some two million tonnes to 24 million tonnes in 1996 due in the main to poor weather during the spring and summer, he said in an interview at a Paris food industry fair.
A long, cold winter delayed spring sowings while the start of the harvest was disrupted by rain in August.
Wheat is heavily used in Poland for feeding animals. Some 60 percent of the domestic wheat production and 75 percent of wheat imports goes into feed, Kreft said.
But despite a lower domestic crop, Poland plans to import less wheat this season, he said.
"We expect to import less than the 1.5 million tonnes of wheat we imported in the 1995/96 season," he said.
Since September Poland has bought around 500,000 tonnes of wheat from the European Union (EU), he said, confirming grain industry reports. Traders say the wheat has been moving mainly from Germany.
Kreft said the buying spree followed a move by the EU to restore subsidies on wheat to dispose of a bumper EU crop.
The EU restored the subsidies in September after a 16-month suspension during which subsidies gave way to export taxes for a while, in a move to curb domestic commodity inflation.
Kreft said the EU export taxes had caused some difficulties for Poland's domestic grain industry.
"The EU tax caused some supply problems," he said.
Further buying for the 1996/97 season would now depend on world market prices, he said.
But he added that import business would be helped by a Polish state decision to suspend an import tax on wheat until the end of 1996.
Poland suspended duties on wheat, barley, rye and oats at the beginning of 1996. The decision was part of a broad set of measures tied to the Warsaw government's anti-inflationary plan.
Of Poland's total grain import needs during 1996/97, the London-based International Grains Council projects wheat imports of 300,000 tonnes, unchanged from the previous season.
Wheat production fell to 8.3 million tonnes this year from 8.7 million tonnes in 1995, the inter-governmental watchdog said in its latest market report.
